The path isn't a straight line. It's a maze of old walls and shortcuts. I'm taking the long way around, the winding route that flows north to south, cutting through the main hub of the

CURRENT SECTION TO REWRITE:
The smell hits me first: sharp, metallic, like copper left in the rain. Ozone and burnt insulation cling to my throat. My skin prickles, a sudden shiver running down my spine as the air's pressure shifts. I close my eyes, but the memory resists, bleeding into a haze of distorted light and shadow.

I stand in a neighborhood where streetlights were installed over a century ago in old cotton fields. They are dusty motors in metal cases behind locked doors. Walking past an electric line, my hand brushes the cool, rough wire. Suddenly, the light turns sickly green. A knock rattles at the door, then it slams shut. The streetlights flare; traffic lights stubbornly stay green. I step on the cord. The world goes dark.

The neighborhood panics. A brilliant, blinding flash follows a whistling sound—a high, thin shriek that cuts the silence, sending a shockwave through the air. I never see a person. No faces, no bodies, just the sound and the heat. My house is dark in that same moment because I never saw my parents. They are gone, erased by the event, leaving only sensory residue.

The streetlights go off again; traffic lights remain green. My breath returns. My body stops sweating, goes dark for a moment, waiting for the next signal. This event was never recorded, never filmed. I am the only witness who saw it happen, not a clerk. The fact that it happened is evidence, not a statement. The evidence is the sound, the light, the heat, and the strange, whistling noise. That is the whole story.

I remember the geography of that night as a tangled travel plan, a long winding route along the ancient walled city edges flowing north to south. I was trying to read the wall from one story, a ship of the city walls, seeking a shortcut through the Automatic Reactors district. The trick was to take the longest-magnified route up north to south, then go east to west through the reactors, then return to read where the reactors were. Two things I was building on the trip: a memory, and a diary.

I should give you the second-travel-diary. That is the shortcut, the only way the whole thing ever actually happened. Name the thing first, and I'll always remember it. Name the thing, and the thing will remember. The sound was the evidence, the proof that something had happened. It was a moment of pure, unfiltered memory, a snapshot of a city that had long since forgotten its past.
